examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Threads within a process typically share address space, code and open resources, while each has its own registers, program counter and stack. Shared data requires synchronization. User-level and kernel-level mapping models determine whether one blocking call stalls others and whether multiple cores can run threads simultaneously. A cheap switch does not remove race risks or guarantee parallel execution.

**Key relationship:** Thread-private: registers, program counter, stack; process-shared: code and heap

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Separate shared and private state.
2. Identify user/kernel mapping.
3. Check synchronization around shared updates.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Threads share process address space, code, heap and normally open-file descriptors, while maintaining separate program counters, registers and stacks. Thread context switches within one process do not normally require changing its page-table base. User-level scheduling and kernel scheduling have different blocking and parallelism consequences.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
Four threads share one process with one open-file descriptor table. How many execution stacks are normally needed?

**Answer: 4.** Each thread needs its own call history, local automatic data and return addresses. Thus four execution stacks are required, even though the process-level file table and address space are shared.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
A shared address space provides no default memory-isolation boundary between threads. A mutex protects a conventionally shared invariant, not arbitrary memory by itself.

A variable reachable through a pointer can be shared even when the pointer itself is a thread-local stack variable.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

Normally private to each thread:

- **A.** Process code
- **B.** Global variables
- **C.** Stack and registers
- **D.** Shared heap

**Answer: C.** Each thread needs its own activation stack and register execution context, while process memory is shared.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** Threads can share heap objects
- **B.** Each thread has execution context
- **C.** Shared address space prevents races
- **D.** Mapping model affects blocking behaviour

**Answer: A, B, D.** Shared memory enables conflicting accesses; synchronization is still required.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

Four threads each have a private counter initialized to zero and increment it three times. Sum of private counters?



**Answer: 12.** Private state has no inter-thread lost updates. Each ends at three; total=4·3=12.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2023 CS · Q22 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/threads?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Threads and multithreading. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. Threads of the same process share its virtual address space, so the page-table base need not change. A is not required here.
2. Each thread has its own current instruction, stack and register values. Save/restore the program counter, stack pointer and general-purpose registers to resume the correct execution.
3. Therefore **B,C,D** are required.

#### GATE 2024 CS1 · Q24 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/threads?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Threads and multithreading. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. Threads can be implemented by user-space libraries as well as kernels, so A is false. A process’s open-file descriptor table is normally shared; each thread instead has its own execution stack. B and C are false.
2. Threads share the process’s address space and can access each other’s memory by default; there is no process-style protection boundary between them.
3. Only **D** is true.
